analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to legally import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and other approved countries.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 36 cosponsors from both parties but never got a vote; it died in a Senate committee at the end of 2008.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite federal drug law to let registered pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada, Australia, Japan, New Zealand, Switzerland, and the European Union. It builds in safety checks — registration, inspections, chain-of-custody records, and recalls — and bans drug companies from punishing anyone who imports. Its stated aim is to close the price gap: by the bill's own findings, Americans pay up to five times more for the same drugs sold abroad.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially uninsured and underinsured people who pay full price at the pharmacy. It would also open a legal market for Canadian and other foreign pharmacies and for U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers willing to act as registered importers.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that Americans pay up to 5 times more to fill prescriptions than consumers in other countries, and that the Congressional Budget Office has found drug prices are 35 to 55 percent lower in other developed countries [S3].

It waives the federal restriction on importing prescription drugs, allowing registered importers and individuals buying for personal use (up to a 90-day supply) to bring in qualifying drugs from Canada and other permitted countries [S2].
It requires the FDA to publish a public list of registered exporters and to educate consumers about importation, giving patients a verified way to buy from vetted foreign pharmacies [S2].

It makes it illegal for manufacturers to charge exporters higher prices, cut off supplies, or take any action to restrict or delay importation, and states that reselling in the U.S. drugs properly sold abroad is not patent infringement [S2].

The bill builds in safety machinery: FDA inspection of exporter facilities at least 12 times a year, verified chains of custody, track-and-trace markings on shipments, recall coordination, and refusals of admission for suspect shipments [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would face a large share of their U.S. revenue exposed to competition from lower-priced sales of the same products abroad. Importers and exporters pay registration and inspection fees (capped at 2.5 percent of drug value) that fund the FDA program. Foreign governments that run price-regulated systems could see upward pressure on their drug prices if U.S. demand draws down supply.

drawbacks.text: Opponents have long argued that imported drugs carry safety risks — counterfeit, mishandled, or mislabeled products could reach patients through foreign supply chains, and the bill's own design (fee-funded inspections, chain-of-custody verification) reflects how hard that is to police [S2].

The bill requires manufacturers to file detailed notices about any difference between their foreign and U.S. versions of a drug and forbids them from creating differences to block importation — a heavy compliance burden that manufacturers said would be costly and burdensome [S2].

Large-scale importation could put upward pressure on prices in Canada and other permitted countries, where governments regulate drug prices, and could strain those countries' supply — a cost borne by their citizens, not Americans.

The safety program is funded by fees on importers and exporters and by FDA administration; if the industry resists cooperating, enforcement would fall on a regulator charged with verifying thousands of foreign transactions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The price gap the bill targets is large and documented — Americans pay the highest brand-drug prices in the world for products sold far cheaper abroad. The real cost is that a regulated importation system is complex to run safely, and a failure could put bad drugs in pharmacies. The bill's response — inspections, verified custody chains, track-and-trace markings, and recall agreements — is a serious attempt to manage that risk rather than ignore it. The tradeoff favors patients, but the system would have needed sustained regulatory resources to work as written.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never acted on it, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 10, 2007, by Senator Byron Dorgan with 29 original cosponsors including Republicans Olympia Snowe, Chuck Grassley, John McCain, and Arlen Specter, and was read twice and referred to the HELP Committee [S3].
It drew 36 cosponsors in total — 29 Democrats, 6 Republicans, and 1 Independent [S4].
On March 7, 2007, a Commerce subcommittee held a hearing on pharmaceutical market access — the only further congressional action recorded; the bill's referral committee never reported it [S5].
No floor vote ever occurred in either chamber, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the U.S. market closed to cheaper foreign sales of their own products, and Americans continued paying the highest brand-drug prices in the world.

sides.party_line_note: Support was strongly bipartisan — 36 cosponsors split 29 Democrats, 6 Republicans, and 1 Independent — so the bill was not killed by a party-line vote but by committee inaction.

industries.note: The bill exposes their U.S. prices to competition from the same drugs sold 35-55 percent cheaper abroad and bans them from cutting off or punishing exporters. Their loss of U.S. pricing power is the direct source of savings for patients.

industries.industry: Foreign and internet pharmacies and registered drug exporters
industries.note: The bill creates a legal, registered pathway for Canadian and other foreign pharmacies to sell to Americans, with a published list of vetted exporters. Their new business is the channel through which patients get cheaper drugs.

They could become registered importers and pass imported savings to customers, but they would face new fees ($10,000 registration plus inspection fees) and compliance duties. Some current distribution intermediaries would also face new competition.

industries.industry: Payment processors and credit card networks
industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful to run transactions with unregistered foreign pharmacies through payment systems, adding a compliance duty but closing a channel used by rogue sellers that victimize patients.
